la:verb:subeo.gloss: to go under, come under; enter
senses: to go under, come under; enter
to come or go up to, approach, draw near, advance or proceed to a place; come or go on
to submit to, undergo, bear, endure
to approach stealthily, sneak up on
to go up, mount, climb, scale
la:verb:subeo.html:
sŭb-ĕo, ĭi, ĭtum, īre (
perf. subīvit, ; : subivimus, Claud. ap. dub.), v. n. and a., to come or go under any thing; to come or go up to, to approach, draw near, advance or proceed to a place; to come or go on; to follow, succeed; to go down, sink; to come up, spring up (cf. succedo).
Neutr.
Lit.
In gen.: subire sub falas,: in nemoris latebras,; cf.: in aliquem locum, to enter, Auct. B. Alex. 74, 4: in adversum Romani subiere,: in adversos montes,: testudine factā subeunt,advance,: Albani subiere ad montes,: subire ad portam castrorum,; cf.: ad urbem subeunt,; ; ; and: subeundum erat ad hostes,: ad tecta subibant,.—With dat.: muro subibant,; so, muro,: portu Chaonio (with accedere urbem),: luco,: dumis,: ingenti feretro,: age cervici inponere nostrae: Ipse subibo umeris,: per vices subeunt elephanti,: pone subit conjux,follows,; so ; cf.: dexterae alae sinistra subiit,: subeuntis alii aliis in custodiam,; and: subiit argentea proles,: subit ipse meumque Explet opus,succeeds me, takes my place,: Volscus saxa objacentia pedibus ingerit in subeuntes,climbing,: vel eodem amne vel Euphrate subire eos posse,i. e. sail up stream,; cf.: adverso amne Babylona subituros,.—
Of things: stamen a stando: subtemen, quod subit stamini, Müll.: cum luna sub orbem solis subisset,: tertio die mixtum flumini subibat mare,: venae nonnumquam incipiente febre subeunt,the pulse sinks,: subeunt herbae,come up, spring up,; so, barba,i. e. sprouts, grows,: subisse aquam in caelum,.—
In partic., to come on secretly, to advance or approach stealthily, to steal upon, steal into (poet.), ; ; .—
Trop.
In gen., to come in, succeed, take place; to enter stealthily, come secretly or by degrees: in quarum locum subierunt inquilinae impietas, perfidia, impudentia, Varr. ap. : fugere pudor verumque fidesque: In quorum subiere locum fraudesque dolique,: pulchra subit facies,: subit ecce priori Causa recens,: an subit (amor) et tacitā callidus arte nocet?: subeunt morbi

tristisque senectus, : namque graves morbi subeunt segnisque senectus,; cf.: duo pariter subierunt incommoda,arise, come up,: ne subeant animo taedia justa tuo,: regio, quā vero ipsa subit ad Medos,approaches,. —

In partic., to come into the mind, to occur, suggest itself: omnes sententiae verbaque omnia sub acumen stili subeant et succedant necesse est,: cum in loca aliqua post tempus reversi sumus, quae in his fecerimus, reminiscimur personaeque subeunt,: cum subeant audita aut cognita nobis,: subit umbra,: subeunt illi fratresque parensque,. 542: subiit cari genitoris imago ... subiit deserta Creusa Et direpta domus et parvi casus Iuli,; : subeant animo Latmia saxa tuo,: ne subeant animo taedia,: quantum subire animo sustinueris, tantum tecum auferas,to grasp with the mind,, ext. 7.—
Subit, with subj.- or rel.-clause (poet. and in postAug. prose), : quo magis ac magis admirari subit,; 35, 7, 31, § 49: misereri sortis humanae subit,: quid sim, quid fuerimque subit,.
Act.
Lit.
In gen., to come or go under, to enter; to submit to; to approach, etc.: exercitatissimi in armis, qui inter annos XIV. tectum non subissent,had not come under a roof,: tecta,; : jam subeunt Triviae lucos atque aurea tecta,: limina victor Alcides subiit,: domos,: penates,: macra cavum repetes artum, quem macra subisti,: cum novies subiere paludem,had plunged under,; : et juncti currum dominae subiere leones,: leones jugum subeant,: asellus gravius dorso subiit onus,i. e. submits to, receives,: subire iniquissimum locum,: iniquum locum, Auct. B. Alex. 76, 2; : collem,to go up, mount, climb, scale,: consules utrimque aciem subeuntium jam muros adgrediuntur,: muros,: impositum saxis Anxur,: si subeuntur prospera castra, et saep.: perfurit, Fadumque Herbesumque subit,comes up to, attacks, assails,; cf.: interim fallendus est judex et variis artibus subeundus,: precibus commota Tonantem Juno subit,approaches,: subit ille minantem,: Aeneae mucronem,: qui procul hostium conspectu subibant aquam,: Hispo subit juvenes, i. e. paedicat,.—
Of things: umbra subit terras,: quos (lucos) aquae subeunt et aurae,enter,: montes Trasimenus,: litora pelagus, Mel. praef. 2: mare quod Ciliciam subit,: radices (petrae) Indus amnis subit,: clarus subit Alba Latinum,succeeds, (al. clarus subit ecce Latinum Epytus); cf. : furcas subiere columnae,come into the place of, succeed,: aqua subit altitudinem exortus sui,rises to, reaches,: lunamque deficere cum aut terram subiret aut sole premeretur,.—
In partic., to approach secretly, to steal upon or into (cf. supra, I. A. 2.): multi Nomine divorum thalamos subiere pudicos,: subit furtim lumina fessa sopor,.—
Trop.
In gen. (very rare): sera deinde poenitentia subiit regem,came upon, overtook,.—
In partic.
To come into, enter, occur to one's mind (cf. supra, I. B. 2.): deinde cogitatio animum subiit, indignum esse, etc.,: ut beneficiorum memoria subiret animos patrum,: spes animum subibat deflagrare iras vestras posse,: otiosum animum aliae cogitationes,: majora intellectu animos non subibunt,: mentem subit, quo praemia facto, etc.,; : subit ergo regem verecundia,: me recordantem miseratio,: feminas voluptas, id. Pan. 22, 3: horum cogitatio subibat exercitum,.—
To follow in speech, interrupt, answer (post - class. and rare): dicturum plura parentem Voce subis,: subit ille loquentem talibus,; .—
(The figure taken from stooping under a load, under blows, etc.) To subject one's self to, take upon one's self an evil; to undergo, submit to, sustain, endure, suffer it (class.; a favorite expression of Cic.): omnes terrores periculaque omnia succurram atque subibo,: omnia tela intenta in patriam subire atque excipere,; cf.: quis est non ultro appetendus, subeundus, excipiendus dolor?: subire vim atque injuriam,: inimicitiae sunt: subeantur,: maximas rei publicae tempestates,: invidiam, pericula, tempestates,: nefarias libidinum contumelias turpitudinesque,: potentiam, victoriam,: contumeliarum verbera,: majora Verbera,: non praecipuam, sed parem cum ceteris fortunae condicionem,: fortunam,: judicium multitudinis imperitae,: odium eorum,: usum omnium,: aliquid invidiae aut criminis,: quemque casum,: quamvis carnificinam,: dupli poenam,: legis vim,: summae crudelitatis famam,; cf.: minus sermonis,: poenam exsilii,: simultates,: offensas,: periculum,: jam tum peregrinos ritus novā subeunte fortunā,. —With inf., to attempt, try, undertake: adversa tela pellere,: clavum torquere,.— Hence, sŭbĭtus, a, um, P. a., that has come on suddenly or unexpectedly, i. e. sudden, unexpected (freq. and class.; cf.: repens, improvisus): res subita,: in rebus tam subitis,: maris subita tempestas,: subita et improvisa formido,: laetitia, etc.,: subita pugna, non praeparata,: ut sunt Gallorum subita et repentina consilia,: novae rei ac subitae admiratio,: bellum,: incursiones hostium,: ministeria belli,: imbres,: vis,; : res,: mors,: casus,; : tristia,: silentium,: miles, hastily collected (opp. vetus expertusque; syn. subitarius),; cf.: aqua mulsa subita ac recens (opp. inveterata),: imagines non subitae, not newly sprung up, i. e. old, ancient, : homo,rash,: clivi, sudden, i. e. steep, .—Esp., = subito (post-Aug.): non percussor ille subitus erumpet?; so, manūs dux Trapezuntem subitus irrupit,: subitum inopinatumque venisse,: evadere,.—
As subst.: sŭbĭtum, i. n., a sudden or unexpected thing, a sudden occurrence, etc.: Lesbonicum foras evocate: ita subitum'st, propere eum conventum volo,; cf.: subitum est ei remigrare,: si tibi subiti nihil est,: in subito,.—In plur.: ut subitis ex tempore occurrant,; cf.: etiam fortes viros subitis terreri,: quamvis non deficeretur ad subita extemporali facultate,: si repentina ac subita dominantur,: sive meditata sive subita proferret, whether he spoke after deliberation or off-hand, .—With gen.: ad subita rerum,: ad subita belli,; ; .—
Adverb., suddenly, unexpectedly: per subitum erumpit clamor,; so, per subitum,; ; ; 14, 330; 15, 145; 15, 404: in subitum,: ad subitum, praef. med.—Hence, adv.: sŭbĭtō, suddenly, unexpectedly (freq. and class.; cf.: repente, extemplo, ilico): ut subito, ut propere, ut valide tonuit! ; cf. : nova res subito mihi haec objecta est,: ita abripuit repente sese subito,: subito tanta te impendent mala,: cum tot bella subito atque improviso nascantur,: ex oculis subito fugit,: cum subito ecce,: ut subito nostras Hymen cantatus ad aures Venit,; : subito deficere,: quod serenā nocte subito candens et plena luna defecisset,: tantus subito timor omnem exercitum occupavit,: subito opprimi,: si vespertinus subito te oppresserit hospes, et. saep.: subito dicere,without preparation, extempore,: quod vox et gestus subito sumi non potest,: neque potest quisquam nostrum subito fingi,: aliquid subito ex tempore conjectura explicare,; so, dicere,; : inventa (opp. domo allata),: cum subito evaserunt,: tam subito copias contrahere non potuit,so quickly,.

senses: about, around (time); just before, just after, shortly before, shortly after
under, up to, up under, close to (of a motion)
la:prep:sub.html:
sŭb (on the form sus from subs
v.infra, III.), prep. with acc. and abl. [perh. for es-ub, ens-ub, = ἐνς (εις) and ὑπό; Sanscr. upa; cf. ], under.
With abl., to point out the object under which a thing is situated or takes place (Gr. ὑπό, with dat. or gen.), under, below, beneath, underneath.
Of space: si essent, qui sub terrā semper habitavissent ... nec tamen exissent umquam supra terram,; : sub aquā,: sub vestimentis,; ; cf.: saepe est sub palliolo sordido sapientia, Caecil. ap. : ingenium ingens Inculto latet hoc sub corpore,: sub pellibus hiemare,; cf. : manet sub Jove frigido Venator,: sub divo moreris,: vitam sub divo agat, (v. divus, II.): sub terrā vivi demissi sunt,: sub hoc jugo dictator Aequos misit,: pone (me) sub curru nimium propinqui Solis, et saep.— Trop.: non parvum sub hoc verbo furtum latet,.—
Transf., of lofty objects, at the foot of which, or in whose immediate neighborhood, any thing is situated, under, below, beneath, at the foot of, at, by, near, before: sub monte consedit,; so, sub monte considere,: sub colle constituere,: sub montis radicibus esse, al.: sub ipsis Numantiae moenibus,: est ager sub urbe,; so, sub urbe,, 26; ; : sub Veteribus,: sub Novis, Orell. N. cr.; Goer. N. cr.; cf. Müll.: sub basilicā, et saep.—Trop.: sub oculis domini suam probare operam studebant,: omnia sub oculis erant,; cf. : classem sub ipso ore urbis incendit,.—
Of time, in, within, during, at, by: ne sub ipsā profectione milites oppidum irrumperent,: sub decessu suo,: sub luce,; ; : sub eodem tempore,: sub somno, al.—
In other relations, where existence under or in the immediate vicinity of any thing may be conceived.
Under, in rank or order; hence, next to, immediately after: Euryalumque Helymus sequitur; quo deinde sub ipso Ecce volat calcemque terit jam calce Diores,.—
In gen., of subjection, domination, stipulation, influence, effect, reason, etc., under, beneath, with: omnes ordine sub signis ducam legiones meas,under my standards,: sub armis vitam cernere, Enn. ap. Müll. (Trag. v. 297 Vahl.); so, sub armis,; : sub sarcinis,; : sub onere, et saep.—
Trop., under, subject to, in the power of; during, in the time of, upon, etc.: sub Veneris regno vapulo, non sub Jovis,: sub regno esse,: sub imperio alicujus esse,: sub dicione atque imperio alicujus esse,; Auct. B. Alex. 66, 6; ; ; ; cf.: sub Corbulone Armenios pellere,: sub manu alicujus esse, Planc. ap. ; sub rege,; : sub Hannibale,: sub dominā meretrice,: sub nutrice,: sub judice lis est,: praecipua sub Domitiano miseriarum pars erat,during the reign of,: scripsit sub Nerone novissimis annis,: gnarus sub Nerone temporum,; et saep.: sub vulnere,from the effects of the wound,; cf.: sub judice,under,: nullo sub indice,forced by no betrayer,.—So in certain phrases where the simple abl. is more freq.: sub pacto abolitionis dominationem deponere,: sub condicione, Weissenb. ad loc.: sub condicionibus,: sub eā condicione, ne cui fidem meam obstringam,: sub eā condicione, si esset, etc.,; so, sub condicione, ut (ne, si, etc.),; ; ; ; : sub specie (= specie, or per speciem): sub specie infidae pacis quieti,; ; : sub tutelae specie,; ; cf.: sub nomine pacis bellum latet,: sub alienis auspiciis rem gerere,: sub lege, ne,: sub exceptione, si,: sub poenā mortis,: servitutis, et saep.: sub frigido sudore mori, —
With acc., to point out the object under which a thing comes, goes, extends, etc. (Gr. ὑπό, with acc.), under, below, beneath.
Of space, usually with verbs of motion: et datores et factores omnes subdam sub solum,: manum sub vestimenta deferre,: cum tota se luna sub orbem solis subjecisset,: exercitum sub jugum mittere,; ; Dietsch ad loc.: sub furcam ire,: sub divum rapere,: sub terras ire,. —Trop.: sub judicium sapientis et delectum cadunt,: quae sub sensus subjecta sunt,: quod sub aurium mensuram aliquam cadat,: columbae Ipsa sub ora viri venere,: quod sub oculos venit,.—Rarely with verb of rest: quidquid sub Noton et Borean hominum sumus,.—
Transf. (cf. supra, I. A. 2.), of lofty objects, to the foot of which, or into whose immediate neighborhood, any thing comes, or near to which it extends, under, below, beneath, to, nearto, close to, up to, towards, etc.: sub montem succedunt milites,: sub ipsum murum fons aquae prorumpebat,: missi sunt sub muros,: Judaei sub ipsos muros struxere aciem,; : aedes suas detulit sub Veliam,: arat finem sub utrumque colonus,: jactatus amnis Ostia sub Tusci,: (hostem) mediam ferit ense sub alvum,: sub orientem secutus Armenios,.—
Of time, denoting a close approximation.
Before, towards, about, shortly before, up to, until: Pompeius sub noctem naves solvit,; so, sub noctem,; ; ; ; : sub vesperum,; : sub lucem,; : sub lumina prima,: sub tempus edendi,: sub dies festos,: sub galli cantum,: usque sub extremum brumae intractabilis imbrem,: simulacra Visa sub obscurum noctis,: prima vel autumni sub frigora,: quod (bellum) fuit sub recentem pacem,.—
After, immediately after, just after, immediately upon: sub eas (litteras) statim recitatae sunt tuae,; cf. Cael. ap. : sub haec dicta omnes procubuerunt,: sub adventum praetoris,; ; : sub hanc vocem fremitus variantis multitudinis fuit,: sub hoc erus inquit,hereupon,.—
In other relations, in which a coming under any thing may be conceived: lepide hoc succedit sub manus negotium,comes to hand, convenient,: sub manus succedere,; : sub manum submittere, at hand, convenient, Auct. B. Afr. 36, 1: sub ictum venire,: sub manum annuntiari, (al. sub manu; cf. supra, I. C.): sub legum et judiciorum potestatem cadere,: sub populi Romani imperium dicionemque cadere, (1, 2): incolas sub potestatem Atheniensium redigere,: matrimonium vos sub legis superbissimae vincula conicitis,: sub unum fortunae ictum totas vires regni cadere pati,.—
In composition, the b remains unchanged before vowels and before b, d, j, l, n, s, t, v. Before m and r it is frequently, and before the remaining consonants, c, f, g, p, it is regularly assimilated. Yet here the MSS. vary, as in ob, ad, in, etc. Before some words commencing with c.p, t, it assumes the form sus, by the rejection of the b from a collateral form subs (analog. to abs); e. g. suscipio, suscito, suspendo, sustineo, sustuli, sustollo. Before s, with a following consonant, there remains merely su in the words suspicio, suspicor, suspiro; cf., however: substerno, substituo, substo, substruo al.; v. esp. Neue, Formenl. 2, 775 sqq.—
In composition, sub denotes,
Lit., a being situated or contained under, a putting or bringing under, or a going in under any thing: subaeratus, subcavus; subdo, subigo, subicio; subhaereo, subaperio; subedo.—
Hence, also, a concealing or being concealed behind something; a secret action: subnoto, surripio, suffuror, subausculto, suborno. —
Transf., a being placed or ranked under: subcenturio, subcurator, subcustos, etc.; or a being or doing any thing in a lower or inferior degree, a little, somewhat, rather, slightly: subabsurdus, subagrestis, subalbus, etc.; subaccusare, subirascor, etc.

la:verb:subsum.gloss: to be under, among or behind
senses: to be under, among or behind
la:verb:subsum.html:
sub-sum, no
perf., esse, v. n., to be under, among, or behind; to be near, close, or at hand (class.): ubi non subest, quo praecipitet ac decidat,there is nothing underneath,; ; cf. : si quid intra cutem subest ulceris, Planc. ap. : subucula subest tunicae,: nigra subest lingua palato,: suberat Pan ilicis umbrae : cum sol Oceano subest,.—
To be near, to be at hand, of places and persons: mons suberat,: montes,: vallis,: planities,: vicina taberna,: templa mari,; cf.: regnum Ariobarzanis illi, Sall. Ep. Mithrid. ad Arsac. med.: me subesse propinquis locis, Planc. ap. .—
Transf., of time, to be near or at hand, to approach: nox jam suberat,was near,; so, hiems,: dies comitiorum,.—
Trop., to be underneath, be at the bottom, be or exist under, lie concealed in: in quā (legatione) periculi suspitio non subesset,: in quā re nulla subesset suspitio,; and simply suspitio,: eadem causa subest,: causa aliqua,; cf.: si his vitiis ratio non subesset,: ratio,; : si negabimus temere famam Naxi solere, quin subsit aliquid,: si ulla spes salutis nostrae subesset,: nam illi regi amabili, Cyro, subest ad inmutandi animi licentiam crudelissimus ille Phalaris,; : saepe solent auro multa subesse mala,are hid under, exist under,: subest silentio facinus, et saep.— Poet.: notitiae suberit amica tuae,will be subject to your cognizance,.

la:verb:subedo.gloss: to eat from under, wear away
senses: to eat from under, wear away
la:verb:subedo.html:
sŭb-ĕdo, ēdi, 3, v. a.,
to eat, waste, or wear away below: e scopulo, quem rauca subederat unda,; .

la:noun:subsidium.html:
subsĭdĭum, ii, n.
subsideo
.
Milit. t. t.
Orig., the troops stationed in reserve in the third line of battle (behind the principes), the line of reserve, reserve-ranks, triarii: subsidium dicebatur, quando milites subsidebant in extremā acie labentique aciei succurrebant. Quod genus militum constabat ex iis, qui emeruerant stipendia, locum tamen retinebant in exercitu: quae erat tertia acies triariorum, Müll.; cf.: subsidium, quod postpositum est ad subveniendum laborantibus, ib.: triarii quoque dicti, quod in acie tertio ordine extremis subsidio deponebantur: quod hi subsidebant, ab eo subsidium dictum, ib. (very rare): subsidia et secundam aciem adortus,: jaculatores fugerunt inter subsidia ad secundam aciem,: impulsa frons prima et trepidatio subsidiis illata,: in subsidiis pugnacissimas locaverunt gentes,: in subsidiis positi,.—
A body of reserve, an auxiliary corps, auxiliary forces, etc. (class.; syn.: suppetiae, auxilium): duae cohortes de subsidio procedunt, Sisenn. ap. : rem esse in angusto vidit, neque ullum esse subsidium, quod submitti posset,: neque certa subsidia collocari poterant,: cohortes veteranas in fronte, post eas ceterum exercitum in subsidiis locat,stationed as a reserve,.—
Abstr., support in battle, aid, help, relief, succor, assistance: cum alius alii subsidium ferrent,: funditores Baleares subsidio oppidanis mittit,: missi in subsidium equites,: Italiae subsidio proficisci,; cf. : integros subsidio adducit,: subsidio venire,: commune in Germanos Gallosque subsidium, octo legiones erant,.—
Transf., in gen., support, assistance, aid, help, protection, etc. (syn. adjumentum).
Sing.: abi quaerere, ubi jurando tuo satis sit subsidii,: mihi hoc subsidium (sc. juris interpretationem) jam inde ab adulescentia comparavi, 199; cf.: ut illud subsidium (sc. bibliothe

cam) senectuti parem, : subsidium bellissimum existimo senectuti otium,; cf. : sine talium virorum subsidio resistere,: his difficultatibus duae res erant subsidio,: fidissimum annonae subsidium,: aurum ad subsidium fortunae relictum,: non aliud subsidium quam misericordia Caesaris fuit,: nec tibi subsidio sit praesens numen,.—

Plur.: industriae subsidia,: frumentaria subsidia rei publicae,: sibi subsidia ad omnes vitae status parare,: his ego subsidiis ea sum consecutus,; : ad omnes casus subsidia comparare,to prepare resources, make provision,: mare circa Capreas importuosum et vix modicis navigiis pauca subsidia,.

la:adj:suburbanus.gloss: suburban (near a city, especially near Rome)
senses: suburban (near a city, especially near Rome)
la:adj:suburbanus.html:
sŭb-urbānus, a, um, adj.,
situated near the city of Rome, suburban.
Adj.: rus suburbanum,: fundus,: ager,: gymnasium,: regio Italiae,; cf. Italia,: caulis,: peregrinatio,: crimina, et saep. —
Substt.
sŭburbā-num, i, n. (sc. praedium), an estate near Rome, a suburban villa: malo esse in Tusculano aut uspiam in suburbano,: suburbana amicorum,; ; ; ; , b, 1; ; ; ; ; ; .—
sŭburbāni, ōrum, m., the inhabitants of the towns near Rome, .

la:verb:subicio.gloss: to throw, lay, place, set or bring under or near
senses: to throw, lay, place, set or bring under or near
to subject, submit or subordinate a particular to a general, to range or treat it under, append it
to forge, counterfeit (having that same connotative sense of substituting fake currency or documents for real ones)
la:verb:subicio.html:
sūb-ĭcĭo (less correctly subjĭcĭo; post-Aug. sometimes sŭb-), jēci, jectum, 3, v. a.
sub-jacio
.
Lit., to throw, lay, place, or bring under or near (cf. subdo); in all senses construed with acc. and dat., or with acc. and sub and acc.; not with sub and abl. (v. Madvig. ad ; cf. II. B. 2. infra).
In gen.: si parum habet lactis mater, ut subiciat (agnum) sub alterius mammam. : manum ventri et sub femina (boum),: nonnulli inter carros rotasque mataras ac tragulas subiciebant, discharged their javelins and darts below, i. e. between the wagons and the wheels, : biremes, subjectis scutulis, subduxit,: ligna et sarmenta circumdare ignemque circum subicere coeperunt,; cf.: ignes tectis ac moenibus,: ignem,; Auct. B. Afr. 87, 1; 91, 3; : faces,; ; : bracchia pallae,: eburnea collo Bracchia,: scuto sinistram, Canitiem galeae,: laxiorem sinum sinistro bracchio,: umeros lecto,: pallium togae,: ova gallinis,; : cum tota se luna sub orbem solis subjecisset,: ossa subjecta corpori, et saep: sub aspectum omnium rem subicit,: res sub oculos,: aliquid oculis,; ; : oves sub umbriferas rupes,to place near, close to,: castris legiones,: aciem suam castris Scipionis,: se iniquis locis,: terram ferro,to throw up with the share, to plough up, Moser N. cr.: corpora saltu Subiciunt in equos, throw up, i. e. mount, : pavidum regem in equum,to set,: me e postremo in tertium locum esse subjectum,have been brought, Orell.: copias integras vulneratis defessisque subiciebat, i. e. put in the place of, substituted, Auct. B. Alex. 26, 2.—Hence (poet.): se subicere, to mount, grow: quantum vere novo viridis se subicit alnus,shoots up,: laurus Parva sub ingenti matris se subicit umbrā, Forbig. ad loc.—
In partic.
To hand to, supply: cum ei libellum malus poëta de populo subjecisset,: ipse manu subicit gladios ac tela ministrat,.—

To place under in succession or order, in speaking or writing, i. e. to place after, let follow, affix, annex, append, subjoin (cf.: addo, adicio): post orationis figuras tertium quendam subjecit locum,: longis (litteris) breves subicere,: B litterae absonam et ipsam S subiciendo,: narrationem prooemio,; cf. : cur sic opinetur, rationem subicit,adds, subjoins,: quod subicit, Pompeianos esse a Sullā impulsos, etc.,: a quibusdam senatoribus subjectum est,: subicit Scrofa: De formā culturae hoc dico, etc.,: non exspectare responsum et statim subicere, etc.,: edicto subjecisti, quid in utrumque vestrum esset impensum, et saep.: vix pauca furenti Subicio,i. e. answer, reply,.—
To comprehend under, collect or embrace in: per quam res disperse et diffuse dictae unum sub aspectum subiciuntur,.—
To bring forward, propose, adduce; to bring to mind, prompt, suggest, etc.: si meministi id, quod olim dictum est, subice, Ruhnk.; cf.: cupio mihi ab illo subici, si quid forte praetereo,: subiciens, quid dicerem,: quae dolor querentibus subicit,; : nec tibi subiciet carmina serus amor,: spes est Peliā subjecta creatis,.—Hence, sub-jectus, a, um, P. a.
Of places, lying under or near, bordering upon, neighboring, adjacent: alter (cingulus terrae) subjectus aquiloni,: Heraclea, quae est subjecta Candaviae,: Ossa,: rivus castris Scipionis subjectus,: subjectus viae campus,: Armenia subjecta suo regno (opp. Cappadocia longius remota), Auct. B. Alex. 35, 2; 28, 3: genae deinde ab inferiore parte tutantur subjectae, 2, 57, 143.—
(Acc. to II. B. 1.) Subjected, subject: si quidem Ea (natura deorum) subjecta est ei necessitati,: servitio,: subjectior in diem et horam Invidiae,exposed,: ancipiti fortunae,, ext. 2: species, quae sunt generi subjectae,subordinate,: tum neque subjectus solito nec blandior esto,submissive,; cf.: parcere subjectis et debellare superbos,.—Subst.: sub-jectus, i, m., an inferior, subject: (vilicus), qui, quid aut qualiter faciendum sit, ab subjecto discit,; : Mithridates ab omnibus subjectis singula exquirens, etc.,.—

(sc. verbum), that which is spoken of, the foundation or subject of a proposition: omne quicquid dicimus aut subjectum est aut de subjecto aut in subjecto est. la:verb:subduco.html:
sub-dūco, xi, ctum, 3 (
perf. sync. subduxti, ; inf. subduxe, Poët. ap. ), v. a., to draw from under or from below.
Without the idea of removal.
In gen., to draw or pull up; to lift up, raise (rare): brassicam ad nasum admoveto: ita subducito susum animam, quam plurimum poteris,: aliquid sursum,: cataractam funibus,: subductis (tunicis) usque ad inguen, pulled up (opp. demissis), : supercilia, Turp. ap. ; ; ; ; cf.: subducto voltu, (3, 1), 9.—

With the idea of removal implied, to draw away from among; to take away, lead away, carry off; to withdraw, remove, etc. (class.; syn. subtraho).
In gen.: ubi bullabit vinum, ignem subducito,: lapides ex turri,: rerum fundamenta,: conjux fidum capiti subduxerat ensem,: subduc cibum unum diem athletae,: et sucus pecori et lac subducitur agnis,: pugnae Turnum,; so,: aliquem manibus Graium,: aliquem praesenti periculo,: se pedibus (terra),: se ab ipso Vulnere (fera), et saep. —
Esp.
To purge, evacuate: quoniam is cibus subduceret sensim alvum,; so, alvum,.—
Vela celeriter, to take in, furl, Auct. B. Alex. 45, 3: rem de judicio,.—
Milit. t. t., to draw off forces from one position to another (class.): cohortes aliquot subductas ex dextro cornu post aciem circumducit,: Numidas ex mediā acie,: triarios ex postremā acie,: subductis ordinibus,; cf. : ab his centuriones omnes lectos et evocatos ... in primam aciem subducit,: copias in proximum collem subducit,; : milites pleno gradu in collem,: agmen in aequiorem locum,.—
With the idea of stealth or secrecy.
To take away secretly or by stealth, to steal, hide: Atreus quam (pecudem auream) sibi Thyestem subduxe queritur, Poët. ap. : alicui anulum,: subducta viatica plorat,: post ignem aethereā domo Subductum,: nec mihi rivalis subducit certos amores,: saccularii partem subducunt, partem subtrahunt,: obsides furto,: cubiculum subductum omnibus ventis,secured against,.—
Esp., with se, me, etc., to take one's self away by stealth, withdraw, steal away: tempus est subducere hinc me,: clam te subduxti mihi,: de circulo se subduxit,: modo se subducere ab ipso Vulnere visa fera est,: se clam,; Auct. B. Afr. 93, 1: at nos quaerimus illa (verba), tamquam lateant semper seseque subducant,.—Poet.: neve terra se pedibus subducat,: quā se subducere colles Incipiunt,i. e. to slope down gradually,; cf. mid.: fons subducitur,i. e. loses itself,.—
Trop.
Rationem, to draw up, cast up, reckon, compute, calculate, or balance an account (by subtracting one set of items from another; class.; esp. freq. in Cic.): subduxi ratiunculam, Quantum aeris mihi sit, quantumque alieni siet,; cf.: intus subducam ratiunculam, quantillum argenti mi siet,: subducamus summam,; cf.: assidunt, subducunt: ad numum convenit,.—
In gen.: rationem, to deliberate, calculate: rationibus subductis summam feci cogitationum mearum,: Medea et Atreus ... initā subductāque ratione nefaria scelera meditantes,; cf.: ineundis subducendisque rationibus, id. Fragm. ap. ; for which also, calculis subductis,: bene subductā ratione,: hoc quid intersit, si tuos digitos novi, certe habes subductum,. —Hence, subductus, a, um, P. a.
(Acc. to I. A.) Raised, elevated, upturned: quod vituperones suos subducti supercilii carptores appellavit (Laevius), .—
(Acc. to II. A. 1.) Withdrawn, removed, remote, = remotus (post-Aug. and very rare): terra subductior,.

la:verb:subsisto.html:
sub-sisto, stĭti, 3, v. n. and a.
Neutr., to take a stand or position, to stand still, remain standing; to stop, halt.
Lit.
In gen.: reliqui in itinere substiterant,: in locis campestribus,: in eodem loco,: ad insulam Tauridem, Auct. B. Alex. 45, 1: circa ima (opp. ad summa niti), Quint. prooem. § 20.—Absol.: quo proelio sublati Helvetii audacius subsistere ... coeperunt,: substitit Aeneas et se collegit in arma,; ; ; ; : in aliquo flexu viae ... occultus subsistebat,stationed himself in ambush,; so, occultus,.—
Of things: substitit unda,: amnis,: lacrimae,: ros salsus in alarum sinu,: subsistit radius cubiti,remains in its place,: substitit auspicii lingua timore mali,.—
In partic.
To stay, tarry, abide, remain in a place: locus ubi nationum subsisterent legati, Müll.: erimus ibi die dedicationis: subsistemus fortasse et sequenti,: intra tecta (opp. in aperto vagari),: ut eā die domi subsisteret, orabat,.—
Esp. (late Lat.), to remain alive, ; .—
To make a stand, i. e. to stand firm, hold out; to withstand, oppose, resist: nisi suffulcis firmiter, Non potes subsistere,: Hannibali atque ejus armis, : clipeo juvenis,.—
Of things: quod neque ancorae funesque subsisterent, neque, etc.,stood, held out,.—
Trop.
In gen., to stop, halt, pause; to stay, continue, remain, subsist: subsistere (in dicendo),; : subsistit omnis sententia,: altius ibunt qui ad summa nitentur, quam qui circa ima substiterint,: intra priorem paupertatem subsistere,: equitum nomen subsistebat in turmis equorum publicorum, still remains or subsists only in, etc., : servum quoque et filium familias procuratorem posse habere aiunt: et quantum ad filium familias, verum est: in servo subsistimus,we pause, hesitate, are in doubt,; .—
In partic.
To stand still permanently, i. e. to come to a stop, to cease: substitit ut clamor pressus gravitate regentis,: ingeniumque meis substitit omne malis,: si nihil refert, brevis an longa sit ultima, idem pes erit; verum nescio quo modo sedebit hoc, illud subsistet,.—
(Acc. to A. 2. c.) To stand, withstand, be adequate to, sustain, support a thing: non si Varronis thesauros haberem, subsistere sumptui possem, Brut. ap. : tantis periclis, Claud. ap. : liti,.—
To stand by, support any one (Appuleian): meis extremis aerumnis subsiste,; so , p. 126, 23; 3, p. 139, 28; 5, p. 167, 9; 6, p. 174, 14. —
To stand or hold good, to subsist (late Lat.): non eo minus sententia adversus te latā juris ratione subsistit,; .—
To withstand, make resistance: aut hanc esse veram religionem, cui ad vincendum tanta vis inest, aut illam falsam, quae subsistere non potest,.—
Act. (acc. to I. A. 2. c.), to make a stand against, withstand, encounter any one (very rare): praepotentem armis Romanum subsistere,: feras,.

sub-sīdo, sēdi, sessum, 3 (collat. form acc. to 2d conj., subsīdent, ; ), v. n. and a.

Müll.; and ap. ib.; cf.: subsidunt Hispani adversus emissa tela ab hoste, inde ad mittenda ipsi consurgunt,: partem militum subsidere in subsidiis jussit,; cf.: poplite subsidens,: alii elephanti clunibus subsidentes,: subsedit in illā Ante fores ara,.—

la:verb:subscribo.html:
sub-scrībo, psi, ptum, 3, v. a.

In gen.: statuis inauratis ... subscripsit, Reges ab se in gratiam esse reductos,; cf.: subscripsere quidam L. In partic.
Jurid. t. t., to write down, sign, or subscribe one's name to an accusation (either as principal prosecutor or as seconding others), together with the ground of the charge; hence, in gen., to charge, accuse, prosecute: in L. Popillium subscripsit L. Gellius, quod is pecuniam accepisset, quo innocentem condemnaret, ; cf.: quia parricidii causa subscripta esset,: Gabinium de ambitu reum fecit P. Sulla, subscribente privigno Memmio, fratre Caecilio, etc.,; cf.: Capito Agrippae subscripsit in C. Cassium,; and: accusanti patrono subscripsit,; : cras subscribam homini dicam,: in crimen,; : in crimine,.—
Publicists' t. t., of the censor, to write down, set down, note down the reason of his official censure under or against the name of the person censured: video animadvertisse censores in judices quosdam illius consilii Juniani, cum istam ipsam causam subscriberent,: censor C. Ateium notavit, quod ementitum auspicia subscripsit,: haec quae de judicio corrupto subscripserint, etc.,: ac primum illud statuamus, utrum quia censores subscripserint, ita sit; an quia ita fuerit, illi subscripserint,: quod censores de ceteris subscripserunt,.—
To sign, subscribe a document (by appending one's name or a formula of greeting; perh. not ante-Aug.): omnes (tutores) debent unius editioni subscribere,: rationibus, testamento,; for which, also, rationes,; : si subscripserit in tabulis emptionis, concessisse videtur,: cum de supplicio cujusdam capite damnati, ut ex more subscriberet, admoneretur,; : ipse Commodus in subscribendo tardus et neglegens, ita ut libellis una forma multis subscriberet, in epistolis autem plurimis Vale tantum scriberet,; Wolf (cf. Dio, 57, 11).—
Transf.
To assent to, agree to, approve of any thing: nec quicquam prius pro potestate subscripsit, quam quingenties sestertium ad peragendam Auream domum,: Caesaris irae,: aut gratiae aut odio suo,: odiis accusationibusque Hannibalis,: orationi alicujus,: luxuriae,: si fortuna voto subscripserit,: tuo desiderio, Traj. ap. (96): amoribus alicujus,.—
